title: Receive ye the Holy Ghost (John 20:19–23)
hookLine: he breathes on them: whose sins you forgive; the Church roots confession here

cards: Sunday evening, the same day. Mary has told them what she saw.

And the disciples are in a room with the doors shut, John says, for fear: men who ran away three days ago, jumping at every footstep on the stairs, wondering if they're next, wondering what they'll say if he really is alive.
Not a room full of faith. A room full of nerves and guilt. And then he's simply there, standing in the middle of them.
His first words are today's line.

teach.b: He says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Peace be to you." No accusation. No, where were you?
He shows them his hands and his side, the opened side from two days ago, and they're glad.
Then he says it again, peace be to you, and adds: as the Father hath sent me, I also send you.

And John records something strange and physical: "he breathed on them; and he said to them: Receive ye the Holy Ghost. Whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them: and whose sins you shall retain, they are retained."
That word, breathed, is rare in the Greek Bible. In the Greek translation of Genesis, the same verb is used when God breathes the breath of life into the first human.
Here, on the first day of a new week, Jesus breathes again, and many readers, ancient and modern, hear a new creation beginning. And the first thing the breath is for is forgiveness.
Remember who's in the room: men who denied him and ran. The first gift given to them is the power to forgive.
The Catholic Church roots the sacrament of penance, confession, in this moment.
The Council of Trent taught that here Christ gave the apostles and their successors the power to forgive and retain sins, and the Catechism cites this verse.
That's why, in confession, the priest's words of absolution speak of the Holy Spirit sent among us for the forgiveness of sins, and of pardon and peace.
And that's week seventy-six: I am he, not of this world, Ecce Homo, woman, blood and water, the apostle to the apostles, and the breath of peace.

how: Catholics confess their sins to a priest in the sacrament of penance; the priest prays the words of absolution, which name the Holy Spirit sent for the forgiveness of sins, and sends the penitent away in peace.

o: the risen Jesus giving the Spirit, as in Genesis
a sigh of relief at seeing his friends safe
his last breath as he died on the cross

games.q: the locked room — tap the pairs.
p: as God breathed life into Adam

s: the risen Jesus first scolds the disciples for running away
his first words are peace be to you, twice.
the verb breathed echoes God giving life to the first human
the Greek Genesis 2:7 uses the same rare verb.
the Council of Trent tied this verse to the sacrament of penance
Trent taught the power to forgive and retain sins was given here.

games.q: you're the risen Jesus. the friends who abandoned you are hiding behind locked doors. you appear among them. what do you say first?
games.why: peace be to you. then he shows them his wounds, sends them, breathes on them, and gives them the power to forgive.

practice: Let your breath slow down by itself, cool coming in, warm going out.

If there's something you feel guilty about today, let it be in the room with you, the way the disciples' failures were, and don't argue with it: on each in-breath, receive peace; on each out-breath, let a little of the fear go.
If you pray, hold Jesus's first words, peace be to you; if you don't, just breathe.

wordCard.voice: Breathed. The rare word for what the risen Jesus did to his frightened disciples, echoing the breath of life in Genesis, before sending them to forgive. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: peace be to you. Not an accusation came first, but peace. Day five hundred thirty-two.
